question: How much sleep should healthy adults get?
keyResult: AASM/SRS consensus (modified RAND Appropriateness Method): adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis to promote optimal health. Sleeping less than 7 hours per night on a regular basis is associated with adverse health outcomes. Sleeping more than 9 hours per night on a regular basis may be appropriate for young adults, individuals recovering from sleep debt, and individuals with illnesses; for others it is uncertain whether more than 9 hours is associated with health risk. People concerned they sleep too little or too much should consult their healthcare provider.

citation.authors: Watson NF, Badr MS, Belenky G, et al. (Consensus Conference Panel)
citation.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society

disagreement: AASM/SRS sets a floor ('7 or more hours') with no upper limit, whereas NSF and the Canadian guideline give a 7-9 hour range, and our plain line says '7 to 9 hours'. AASM's own patient site says 'at least 7-8 hours'.
notes: Expert consensus, not a trial. Same statement also published in J Clin Sleep Med (PMID 25979105, PMC4442216). Applies to healthy adults 18-60.

question: What sleep duration does the National Sleep Foundation recommend across the lifespan?
keyResult: 18-member panel (RAND/UCLA Appropriateness Method): newborns 14-17 hours, infants 12-15 hours, toddlers 11-14 hours, preschoolers 10-13 hours, school-aged children 9-11 hours, teenagers 8-10 hours, young adults and adults 7-9 hours, older adults 7-8 hours. Sleep durations outside the recommended range may be appropriate, but deviating far from the normal range is rare.

citation.title: National Sleep Foundation's sleep time duration recommendations: methodology and results summary

disagreement: NSF gives infants 12-15 h while AASM, WHO and Canada give 12-16 h for 4-11/12 months; NSF school-age 9-11 h vs AASM 9-12 h (6-12 y); NSF older adults 7-8 h vs AASM/SRS '7 or more' for all adults.
notes: Expert consensus. NSF receives industry funding (not declared in abstract).

question: Do the NSF 2015 sleep duration recommendations still hold after 10 years of evidence?
keyResult: Review of 133 meta-analyses: 74% (n = 99) were consistent with NSF sleep duration recommendations and the remaining 34 (26%) were inconclusive; none were contradictory for short or long sleep. Most meta-analyses reported nonsignificant sex differences. The review 're-certifies' the NSF recommendations.

citation.authors: Dzierzewski JM, Hirshkowitz M, Dautovich ND, et al.
citation.title: How much sleep do you need: A 10-year systematic review of National Sleep Foundation's sleep duration recommendations and examination of sex differences

notes: Written by NSF staff about NSF's own recommendations; most included meta-analyses focused on adults. Observational evidence dominates.

question: What sleep duration does the CDC tell the public to get, by age?
keyResult: CDC table: newborn 0-3 months 14-17 hours; infant 4-12 months 12-16 hours (including naps); toddler 1-2 years 11-14 hours (including naps); preschool 3-5 years 10-13 hours (including naps); school age 6-12 years 9-12 hours; teen 13-17 years 8-10 hours; adult 18-60 years 7 or more hours; adult 61-64 years 7-9 hours; adult 65 years and older 7-8 hours. Sources: NSF 2015, AASM pediatric 2016, AASM/SRS 2015.

citation.authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
citation.title: About Sleep (page dated May 15, 2024)

disagreement: CDC stitches together AASM and NSF ranges, so the adult band switches from '7 or more' (18-60) to '7-9' (61-64) to '7-8' (65+) depending on which body is cited.
notes: Public-facing summary; no independent evidence review.

question: How much sleep do children and adolescents need (AASM)?
keyResult: AASM pediatric consensus (modified RAND Appropriateness Method); ranges as reproduced by CDC citing this statement: infants 4-12 months 12-16 hours, 1-2 years 11-14 hours, 3-5 years 10-13 hours (all including naps), 6-12 years 9-12 hours, 13-18 years 8-10 hours per 24 hours (CDC table labels teens 13-17).

citation.authors: Paruthi S, Brooks LJ, D'Ambrosio C, et al.
citation.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for Pediatric Populations: A Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine

whatWasRead: abstract (ranges read from the CDC page that cites this statement; full text not retrieved)
disagreement: AASM 6-12 y: 9-12 h vs NSF 9-11 h and Canada 9-11 h (5-13 y). AAP school start time policy cites 8.5-9.5 h for adolescents vs 8-10 h here.
notes: No recommendation for infants under 4 months in the AASM statement (per CDC table, the 0-3 month figure comes from NSF). Verify ranges against the full text before publishing.

question: How much sleep do children under 5 need (Canada)?
keyResult: Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for the Early Years: 14-17 h (0-3 months) or 12-16 h (4-11 months) of good-quality sleep, including naps; toddlers 1-2 years 11-14 h of good-quality sleep, including naps, with consistent bedtimes and wake-up times; preschoolers 3-4 years 10-13 h of good-quality sleep, which may include a nap, with consistent bedtimes and wake-up times. Sleep recommendations graded 'High quality evidence, strong recommendation'.

citation.authors: Tremblay MS, Chaput JP, Adamo KB, et al.
citation.title: Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for the Early Years (0-4 years): An Integration of Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour, and Sleep

notes: GRADE-based; only children 0-4 years. Also recommends screen time not recommended under 2 and no more than 1 h at 2-4 years.

question: What does WHO recommend for sleep in children under 5?
keyResult: WHO 2019: infants under 1 year 14-17 h (0-3 months) or 12-16 h (4-11 months) of good quality sleep, including naps; 1-2 years 11-14 h of good quality sleep, including naps, with regular sleep and wake-up times; 3-4 years 10-13 h of good quality sleep, which may include a nap, with regular sleep and wake-up times. Screen time not recommended for infants and 1-year-olds; for 2-4 years no more than 1 hour, less is better.

citation.title: Guidelines on Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour and Sleep for Children under 5 Years of Age (WHO, Geneva; NCBI Bookshelf NBK541170)

whatWasRead: guideline page (WHO news release summarising the guideline)
disagreement: Matches the Canadian early-years guideline exactly; WHO's 3-4 y band differs from AASM/CDC's 3-5 y band only in age cut-off.
notes: WHO has no sleep-duration guideline for older children or adults.

question: How much sleep do school-aged children and teens need (Canada)?
keyResult: Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for Children and Youth: uninterrupted 9 to 11 hours of sleep per night for those aged 5-13 years and 8 to 10 hours per night for those aged 14-17 years, with consistent bed and wake-up times. No more than 2 hours per day of recreational screen time.

citation.authors: Tremblay MS, Carson V, Chaput JP, et al.
citation.title: Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for Children and Youth: An Integration of Physical Activity, Sedentary Behaviour, and Sleep

disagreement: Canada 9-11 h (5-13 y) vs AASM 9-12 h (6-12 y).
notes: GRADE used for the evidence reviews.

question: How much sleep should adults and older adults get (Canada)?
keyResult: Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines: adults 18-64: 'Getting 7 to 9 hours of good-quality sleep on a regular basis, with consistent bed and wake-up times.' Adults 65+: 'Getting 7 to 8 hours of good-quality sleep on a regular basis, with consistent bed and wake-up times.' Adults 18-64 also: limit sedentary time to 8 hours or less, including no more than 3 hours of recreational screen time.

citation.title: Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for Adults aged 18-64 years and Adults aged 65 years or older: an integration of physical activity, sedentary behaviour, and sleep

disagreement: Upper bound (9 h; 8 h for 65+) like NSF, unlike AASM/SRS '7 or more'.

question: How much sleep do adolescents need, according to the AAP school start time policy?
keyResult: AAP policy: early school start times (before 8:30 am) are a key modifiable contributor to insufficient sleep; AAP urges middle and high schools to aim for start times that allow students to achieve optimal levels of sleep (8.5-9.5 hours).

citation.authors: Adolescent Sleep Working Group; Committee on Adolescence; Council on School Health (American Academy of Pediatrics)
citation.title: School start times for adolescents

disagreement: AAP's 8.5-9.5 h for adolescents is narrower than AASM/NSF/Canada 8-10 h.
notes: Policy statement aimed at schools, not individuals.

question: Is regular sleep timing important for health and performance?
keyResult: NSF sleep timing and variability panel (63 full-text publications; modified Delphi RAND/UCLA, 2 voting rounds) reached consensus that daily regularity in sleep timing is important for health and for performance: 'Consistency of sleep onset and offset timing is important for health, safety, and performance.'

citation.title: The importance of sleep regularity: a consensus statement of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel

notes: Declared COI: panelists received personal fees from the NSF; other industry/grant disclosures listed. Consensus based largely on observational evidence.

question: When weekday sleep is short, is weekend catch-up sleep useful?
keyResult: Same NSF panel reached consensus that, when sleep is of insufficient duration during the week (or work days), catch-up sleep on weekends (or non-work days) is important for health: 'when insufficient sleep is obtained during the week/work days, weekend/non-work day catch-up sleep may be beneficial.'

citation.title: The importance of sleep regularity: a consensus statement of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability panel

disagreement: Tension with our myth line ('doesn't fully make up') and with 'dont-sleep-in-much-on-weekends' and NHLBI's 'limit the difference to about an hour'. NSF says regularity first, but if you are short on sleep, catching up is better than not. Both can be true; the plain line should not imply catch-up sleep is useless.
notes: Panel COI as above.

question: How much should weekend sleep times differ from weekdays?
keyResult: NHLBI: 'Try to keep the same sleep schedule on weeknights and weekends. Limit the difference to no more than about an hour.' Also: 'Go to bed and wake up at the same time every day' and, for children, 'have a set bedtime and a bedtime routine.'

citation.authors: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH)
citation.title: Healthy Sleep Habits (last updated March 24, 2022)

disagreement: NSF regularity panel says weekend catch-up may be beneficial when weekday sleep is short.
notes: Public advice page; no evidence grading.

question: Should you keep the same wake time every day, including after a bad night?
keyResult: NHS insomnia self-help: 'wake up and get out of bed at the same time every day' and 'do not sleep in after a bad night's sleep – stick to your regular sleeping hours instead'. AASM patient site similarly: 'Get up at the same time every day, even on weekends or during vacations.'

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

disagreement: Consistent with stimulus-control instruction '(d) wake up the same time every morning' in the AASM 2021 guideline.

question: Does the AASM count regular timing as part of healthy sleep?
keyResult: AASM position statement: 'In addition to adequate sleep duration, healthy sleep requires good quality, appropriate timing, regularity, and the absence of sleep disorders.'

citation.authors: Ramar K, Malhotra RK, Carden KA, et al.
citation.title: Sleep is essential to health: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine position statement

notes: Position statement by the 2020-2021 AASM board; authors report no conflicts.

question: How long and when should adults nap (NHLBI)?
keyResult: NHLBI: 'Napping during the day may boost your alertness and performance'; 'if you have trouble falling asleep at night, limit naps or take them earlier in the afternoon'; 'Adults should nap for no more than 20 minutes.' 'Napping in preschool-age children is normal and promotes healthy growth and development.'

citation.authors: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH)
citation.title: Healthy Sleep Habits (last updated March 24, 2022)

disagreement: NHS insomnia page says 'do not nap during the day'; Sleep Health Foundation says 15-30 minutes; AASM insomnia guideline's stimulus control includes 'refrain from daytime napping'. Minute limit differs (20 vs 30).

question: What nap length and timing does the Sleep Health Foundation advise?
keyResult: Sleep Health Foundation: 'Naps should be short; 15-30 minutes is best.' 'A long nap late in the day can make it difficult for you to sleep at night.' Suggests napping at the same time each day; people often feel most sleepy around 2-3pm; set the alarm for no longer than 30 minutes. Mentions coffee followed immediately by a nap of about 15 minutes for drowsiness. An evening nap or dozing in front of the TV can make it hard to sleep at night.

citation.title: Napping (fact sheet)

disagreement: SHF allows up to 30 min vs NHLBI 'no more than 20 minutes'; NHS says do not nap (for insomnia).
notes: Fact sheet, no date or evidence grading shown.

question: Should people with insomnia nap?
keyResult: NHS insomnia self-help 'don'ts' include 'do not nap during the day'.

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

disagreement: Direct disagreement with NHLBI (short naps fine, max 20 min) and SHF (15-30 min). Resolvable by audience: no-nap advice is for people with insomnia (matches AASM stimulus control '(e) refrain from daytime napping'); short naps for the general population.
notes: Page is about insomnia, not general sleep health.

question: How long before bed should caffeine stop?
keyResult: Guidance differs by body: NHS insomnia page: 'do not smoke or drink alcohol, tea or coffee at least 6 hours before going to bed'. NHLBI: avoid nicotine and caffeine; 'The effects of caffeine can last up to 8 hours.' CDC and AASM patient pages: avoid caffeine 'in the afternoon or evening'. Sleep Health Foundation: 'Some say caffeine should be avoided for at least 3 to 7 hours before going to sleep. Others say no caffeine after lunch time if you have sleep problems.'

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

whatWasRead: guideline page (NHS, NHLBI, CDC, AASM sleepeducation.org, SHF pages all read)
disagreement: Cut-offs range from 3 h (SHF lower bound) to 6 h (NHS) to 'afternoon' (CDC/AASM) to 'lunch time' (SHF, for people with sleep problems); NHLBI notes effects up to 8 h. Our line 'early afternoon' fits CDC/AASM/NHS for a ~10-11pm bedtime.
notes: No body cites a trial for its specific cut-off; NSF caffeine consensus not found in PubMed.

question: What does the evidence say about caffeine timing as a sleep hygiene rule?
keyResult: Narrative review: caffeine plasma levels peak about 30 minutes after oral intake and a single dose has a half-life of 3-7 hours; in a study of 12 healthy young adults, 400 mg of caffeine taken up to 6 hours before bedtime disturbed both subjective and objective sleep. Overall, epidemiologic and experimental research generally supported links between individual sleep hygiene recommendations and sleep, but direct effects in the general population remain largely untested.

citation.title: The role of sleep hygiene in promoting public health: A review of empirical evidence

notes: Narrative (not systematic) review. The 6-hour study was small (n=12) and used a high dose (400 mg).

question: Does screen use impair sleep, and for whom?
keyResult: NSF panel (16 experts; modified Delphi RAND/UCLA) reached consensus on 5 of 10 statements: screen use in general impairs sleep health in children (5-12) and adolescents (13-19); presleep screen content impairs sleep in children and adolescents; behavioral strategies can reduce negative effects. No consensus that screen use in general or presleep content impairs sleep in adults (20+), and no consensus for any age group that the light from presleep screens impairs sleep.

citation.title: The impact of screen use on sleep health across the lifespan: A National Sleep Foundation consensus statement

disagreement: Public pages give fixed screen cut-offs anyway: CDC and AASM 'at least 30 minutes before bedtime'; Sleep Health Foundation '1-2 hours prior to bed, and if possible, not have them in the bedroom'; NHS 'right before going to bed'; NHLBI 'Use the hour before bed for quiet time' and avoid bright light from TV/computer. The NSF consensus does not support a light-based rationale.
notes: Authors declared no conflicts. Follow-up NSF practical suggestions paper (Grandner MA et al. 2025, Sleep Health, PMID 40701900, doi 10.1016/j.sleh.2025.05.002) has no abstract and is not open access; not read.

question: How long before bed should devices be turned off (CDC/AASM)?
keyResult: CDC: 'Turning off electronic devices at least 30 minutes before bedtime.' AASM patient site: 'Turn off electronic devices at least 30 minutes before bedtime' and 'Limit exposure to bright light in the evenings.'

citation.authors: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
citation.title: About Sleep (page dated May 15, 2024)

disagreement: SHF says 1-2 hours; our line says 'in the hour before bed'.

question: Should screens be kept out of the bedroom?
keyResult: Sleep Health Foundation: turn off all screens 1-2 hours prior to bed, 'and if possible, not have them in the bedroom'; remove distractions such as television, radio and hand-held devices such as phones and laptops from the bedroom.

citation.title: Sleep Hygiene: Good Sleep Habits (fact sheet)

notes: Fact sheet; no evidence grading.

question: What does the AAP say about media and sleep in school-aged children and teens?
keyResult: AAP policy: risks of media use include negative health effects on weight and sleep; recommends families develop a Family Media Use Plan with consistent rules about media use, individualized to developmental stage.

citation.authors: Council on Communications and Media (American Academy of Pediatrics)
citation.title: Media Use in School-Aged Children and Adolescents

notes: Abstract gives no specific bedtime cut-off; full text not read.

question: How dim should evening light be?
keyResult: Expert consensus: during the evening, starting at least 3 hours before bedtime, the recommended maximum melanopic EDI is 10 lux measured at the eye (vertical plane, ~1.2 m height); where possible the white light should be depleted in short wavelengths.

citation.authors: Brown TM, Brainard GC, Cajochen C, et al.
citation.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults

notes: Declared competing interests include lighting-industry funding and consulting for several authors. Unit is melanopic EDI, not ordinary lux, so it can't be quoted to the public as plain 'lux'.

question: How dark should the bedroom be?
keyResult: The sleep environment should be as dark as possible; the recommended maximum ambient melanopic EDI is 1 lux measured at the eye. If activities during the night require vision, the recommended maximum melanopic EDI is 10 lux. Authors suggest blackout blinds and orientation lighting where needed.

citation.authors: Brown TM, Brainard GC, Cajochen C, et al.
citation.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults

notes: Industry COI as above.

question: How much daytime light exposure is recommended?
keyResult: Throughout the daytime, the recommended minimum melanopic EDI is 250 lux at the eye; daylight should be used in the first instance to meet these levels. A stable and regular daily light-dark cycle is also likely to reinforce circadian alignment.

citation.authors: Brown TM, Brainard GC, Cajochen C, et al.
citation.title: Recommendations for daytime, evening, and nighttime indoor light exposure to best support physiology, sleep, and wakefulness in healthy adults

disagreement: Recommendation covers the whole day, not specifically the morning; NHLBI says 'Spend time outside every day'; SHF says 'It is best to be outside in the early part of the day.'
notes: Industry COI as above.

question: What bedroom conditions do public health bodies recommend?
keyResult: CDC: 'Keeping your bedroom quiet, relaxing, and at a cool temperature.' NHLBI: 'Keep your bedroom quiet, cool, and dark (a dim night light is fine, if needed).' NHS: 'make sure your bedroom is dark and quiet – use curtains, blinds, an eye mask or ear plugs if needed' and 'make sure your mattress, pillows and covers are comfortable'.

citation.authors: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH)
citation.title: Healthy Sleep Habits (last updated March 24, 2022)

disagreement: No body gives a temperature number. NHS wording also supports block-outside-light, keep-the-bedroom-quiet and make-your-bed-comfortable.

question: How close to bedtime is exercise OK?
keyResult: NHS insomnia page: 'exercise regularly during the day' but 'do not exercise at least 4 hours before bed'. NHLBI: avoid intense exercise in the hour before bed. Sleep Health Foundation: exercise is good for sleep 'but not just before going to bed'; best times are the morning and before the evening meal; moderate exercise should be avoided in the hour before bed.

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

disagreement: 4 hours (NHS) vs about 1 hour (NHLBI, SHF); our line says 'a couple of hours'.

question: Should people set aside wind-down time before bed?
keyResult: NHS: 'relax at least 1 hour before bed – for example, take a bath or read a book'. NHLBI: 'Use the hour before bed for quiet time' and 'Take a hot bath or use relaxation techniques before bed.' SHF: 'Relax for an hour before going to bed.' AASM patient site: 'Establish a relaxing bedtime routine.'

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

disagreement: All agree on about 1 hour; supports power-down-hour and warm-bath-or-shower-before-bed too.

question: How long should you stay in bed awake before getting up?
keyResult: AASM patient site: 'If you don't fall asleep after 20 minutes, get out of bed. Go do a quiet activity without a lot of light exposure. It is especially important to not get on electronics.' SHF: 'If you are not asleep within 20 to 30 minutes of going to bed you should get up', go to another darkened room and sit quietly. NHS: 'only go to bed when you're sleepy'.

citation.authors: American Academy of Sleep Medicine (Sleep Education); reviewed by Hershner S, Shaikh I
citation.title: Healthy Sleep Habits (updated August 2020)

disagreement: 20 min (AASM) vs 20-30 min (SHF). The AASM 2021 clinical guideline defines stimulus control as 'get out of bed when unable to sleep' with no minute figure.

question: Is stimulus control recommended for chronic insomnia?
keyResult: AASM 2021: 'We suggest that clinicians use stimulus control as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL).' Stimulus control instructions: (a) go to bed only when sleepy; (b) get out of bed when unable to sleep; (c) use the bed/bedroom for sleep and sex only; (d) wake up the same time every morning; (e) refrain from daytime napping.

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

disagreement: Napping rule (e) conflicts with general-public nap advice (NHLBI, SHF).
notes: Funded by AASM; COIs managed and listed. Supports bed-is-for-sleep and get-up-if-you-cant-sleep.

question: How well does stimulus control work on its own?
keyResult: 11 studies (mostly published 1978-1998): stimulus control gave small to large improvements in sleep onset latency and total sleep time vs passive comparators (g = 0.38-0.85); vs active comparators improvements were negligible (g = 0.06-0.30). Authors call it efficacious but call for more robust studies.

citation.authors: Jansson-Fröjmark M, Nordenstam L, Alfonsson S, et al.
citation.title: Stimulus control for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis

notes: Old, small trials; methodological uncertainties noted.

question: What is first-line treatment for chronic insomnia (AASM)?
keyResult: AASM 2021 (GRADE): 'We recommend that clinicians use multicomponent cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (STRONG).' Also conditional recommendations for multicomponent brief therapies, stimulus control, sleep restriction therapy and relaxation therapy. 66 RCTs comparing CBT-I to wait-list, minimal or placebo therapies were identified.

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

notes: Funded by AASM; COIs managed.

question: What does the American College of Physicians recommend first for chronic insomnia?
keyResult: ACP recommends that all adult patients receive CBT-I as the initial treatment for chronic insomnia disorder (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Medication only via shared decision-making if CBT-I alone was unsuccessful (weak recommendation, low-quality evidence).

citation.title: Management of Chronic Insomnia Disorder in Adults: A Clinical Practice Guideline From the American College of Physicians

notes: Based on RCTs published 2004-September 2015.

question: What does the European insomnia guideline recommend (2017)?
keyResult: ESRS 2017: CBT-I is recommended as the first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). Pharmacological intervention can be offered if CBT-I is not sufficiently effective or not available; benzodiazepines, BZRAs and some antidepressants effective short-term (≤4 weeks; weak recommendation). Antihistamines, antipsychotics, melatonin and phytotherapeutics are not recommended. Light therapy and exercise need further evaluation (weak, low-quality evidence). Homeopathy and acupuncture not recommended.

citation.title: European guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia

notes: Based on meta-analyses published until June 2016.

question: What does the 2023 European Insomnia Guideline update recommend?
population: adults with chronic insomnia, including with comorbidities
keyResult: ESRS 2023: CBT-I is recommended as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (including patients with comorbidities), either in-person or digitally (A). Prolonged-release melatonin can be used for up to 3 months in patients ≥ 55 years (B); fast-release melatonin, antihistamines, antipsychotics, ramelteon and phytotherapeutics are not recommended (A). Light therapy and exercise may be useful as adjunct therapies to CBT-I (B). Actigraphy not recommended for routine evaluation (C).

citation.title: The European Insomnia Guideline: An update on the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia 2023

disagreement: Upgrades light therapy and exercise from 'needs further evaluation' (2017) to 'may be useful as adjunct' (2023).
notes: Full text blocked by bot check; sleep-hygiene wording in full text not verified.

question: Is sleep restriction therapy recommended?
keyResult: AASM 2021: 'We suggest that clinicians use sleep restriction therapy as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL).' Defined as limiting time in bed to the patient's sleep duration (from daily diaries), then increasing or decreasing based on sleep efficiency thresholds.

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

disagreement: SHF patient page gives a lay version: 'Spend no more than 8 or so hours in your bed' for poor sleepers.
notes: Clinician-guided; not self-help.

question: Is relaxation therapy recommended for chronic insomnia?
keyResult: AASM 2021: 'We suggest that clinicians use relaxation therapy as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL).' Relaxation therapy = structured exercises to reduce somatic tension (eg, abdominal breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, autogenic training) and cognitive arousal (eg, guided imagery training, meditation).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

notes: Also supports progressive-muscle-relaxation and belly-breathing as named examples.

newAdvice: Sleep tips alone rarely fix long-lasting insomnia; if poor sleep goes on for months, ask about CBT-I.
question: Does sleep hygiene education on its own treat chronic insomnia?
keyResult: AASM 2021: 'We suggest that clinicians not use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for the treatment of chronic insomnia disorder in adults. (CONDITIONAL).' Only 3 RCTs compared sleep hygiene to wait-list, minimal interventions or placebo; resources for sleep hygiene alone 'may divert resources and delay the use of other single- or multicomponent behavioral interventions that are more effective.' Sleep hygiene defined as general recommendations about lifestyle (diet, exercise, substance use) and environment (light, noise, temperature).

citation.authors: Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al.
citation.title: Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline

disagreement: Important framing issue for the whole dataset: most of our concepts are sleep hygiene tips. Bodies recommend them for the general public (CDC, NHS, NHLBI, SHF) but AASM recommends against relying on them alone for chronic insomnia.
notes: Conditional recommendation, low-quality evidence.

newAdvice: Sleep tips alone rarely fix long-lasting insomnia; if poor sleep goes on for months, ask about CBT-I.
question: How effective is sleep hygiene education compared with CBT-I?
population: adults with poor sleep or insomnia
keyResult: 15 studies (12 vs CBT-I, 3 vs mindfulness; none vs sham/no treatment): significant pre-post improvements after sleep hygiene education with small to medium effect size; SHE significantly less efficacious than CBT-I (medium to large difference). Pre-post improvement and SHE-CBT-I difference averaged 5% and 8% in diary sleep efficiency, and two points on the PSQI; only subjective measures were significant.

citation.title: Sleep hygiene education as a treatment of insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis

notes: No sham/no-treatment comparator; no data on adherence or cost.

newAdvice: Sleep tips alone rarely fix long-lasting insomnia; if poor sleep goes on for months, ask about CBT-I.
question: What is the effect of sleep hygiene education on insomnia severity (2025)?
keyResult: 42 RCTs: significant pre-post improvement in ISI (MD = 3.4, 95% CI [2.08, 4.64]), but SHE was inferior to CBT-I (MD = 3.8, 95% CI [2.92, 4.76]), partial CBT-I (MD = 4.5, 95% CI [3.33, 5.60]), exercises (MD = 2.9, 95% CI [0.81, 5.04]) and acupressure (MD = 1.9, 95% CI [0.82, 3.00]). 85.71% of trials had high overall risk of bias.

citation.title: Effects of sleep hygiene education for insomnia: A systematic review and meta-analysis

notes: Authors declare no conflicts. High risk of bias across trials.

question: When should someone see a doctor about poor sleep?
keyResult: NHS: see a GP if changing sleeping habits has not helped, if you've had trouble sleeping for months, or if insomnia makes daily life hard to manage. Short-term insomnia is under 3 months; long-term is 3 months or longer. Treatments: CBT face-to-face or via online self-help; sleeping pills rarely prescribed and only for a few days or weeks at most; pharmacy sleep aids may help for 1 to 2 weeks and shouldn't be taken longer.

citation.title: Insomnia (page last reviewed 19 March 2024)

disagreement: Our line says 'more than a few weeks'; NHS says 'for months' (and defines chronic as 3 months+). SHF/AASM pages say see a doctor if the problem persists, no time given.

question: Should melatonin be used for insomnia?
keyResult: AASM 2017 pharmacologic guideline: 'We suggest that clinicians not use melatonin as a treatment for sleep onset or sleep maintenance insomnia (versus no treatment) in adults. (WEAK).' Same weak 'not use' suggestion for trazodone, tiagabine, diphenhydramine, tryptophan and valerian.

citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Pharmacologic Treatment of Chronic Insomnia in Adults: An American Academy of Sleep Medicine Clinical Practice Guideline

disagreement: ESRS 2023 allows prolonged-release melatonin up to 3 months in people ≥55 but not fast-release melatonin. AASM 2015 endorses timed melatonin for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder. Our line (jet lag/shift work) is outside the scope of these insomnia guidelines.
notes: Weak recommendation; evidence downgraded for publication bias and heterogeneity.

question: Is light therapy or melatonin recommended for delayed sleep-wake phase disorder?
population: people with intrinsic circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorders
keyResult: AASM 2015 (GRADE): positive endorsement (second-tier confidence) of strategically timed melatonin for DSWPD, blind adults with N24SWD, and children/adolescents with ISWRD and neurological disorders; and light therapy with or without behavioral interventions for adults with ASWPD, children/adolescents with DSWPD, and elderly with dementia. Recommendations against melatonin and sleep-promoting medications for demented elderly patients.

citation.title: Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Intrinsic Circadian Rhythm Sleep-Wake Disorders: ASWPD, DSWPD, N24SWD, and ISWRD. An Update for 2015

disagreement: Light therapy for a late body clock is endorsed for children/adolescents with DSWPD, not explicitly for adults; for adults with DSWPD the endorsed option is timed melatonin.
notes: Second-tier ('weak') recommendations.

question: What should night-shift workers do to sleep better?
keyResult: NHLBI shift-work tips: take naps and raise the amount of time available for sleep; keep the lights bright at work; limit shift changes so your body clock can adjust; limit caffeine use to the first part of your shift; remove sound and light distractions in your bedroom during daytime sleep (for example, use light-blocking curtains).

citation.authors: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NIH)
citation.title: Healthy Sleep Habits (last updated March 24, 2022)

notes: Public advice, no evidence grading.

question: Should you avoid watching the clock at night?
keyResult: Sleep Health Foundation: 'If there is a clock in the bedroom, it should be covered to avoid clock-watching.'

citation.title: Sleep Hygiene: Good Sleep Habits (fact sheet)

notes: Only SHF states this among the bodies checked.

question: Is scheduled 'worry time' recommended?
keyResult: Sleep Health Foundation: if you can't switch off your thoughts, 'set aside a ‘worry time’ during the evening' to think about the day, make plans and possible solutions, then don't think about these things until the next day; keep the hour before bed as wind-down time.

citation.title: Sleep Hygiene: Good Sleep Habits (fact sheet)

notes: Does not specify writing it down.

question: How long before bed should the evening meal be?
keyResult: Sleep Health Foundation: 'The evening meal should be at least 2 hours before bedtime'; avoid going to bed on a full or empty stomach; some people find a small snack at bedtime helps. NHLBI: 'Avoid heavy or large meals within a few hours of bedtime. (Having a light snack is okay.)' NHS: 'do not eat a big meal late at night'. AASM: 'If you are hungry at night, eat a light, healthy snack.'

citation.title: Sleep Hygiene: Good Sleep Habits (fact sheet)

disagreement: SHF gives 2 h, NHLBI 'a few hours'. Supports small-snack-before-bed.

question: Is lying awake still restful?
keyResult: Sleep Health Foundation: 'Rest is good – it does not have to be sleep. Don't label yourself as an insomniac as this will increase your worry and frustration.' (Same page advises getting up after 20-30 minutes awake.)

citation.title: Sleep Hygiene: Good Sleep Habits (fact sheet)

disagreement: Sits in tension with stimulus control (get up if unable to sleep); SHF uses it to reduce worry, not as a reason to stay in bed.
notes: Also loosely supports be-kind-to-yourself-after-a-bad-night.

newAdvice: Don't try to cut your sleep into several short blocks a day to need less sleep; it doesn't work and can harm health.
question: Are polyphasic sleep schedules safe?
keyResult: NSF panel reviewed 22 relevant papers (from 40,672 screened) and found no evidence supporting benefits from polyphasic sleep schedules (excluding naps/siestas); they are associated with adverse physical health, mental health and performance outcomes. 'Striving to adopt a schedule that significantly reduces the amount of sleep per 24 hours and/or fragments sleep into multiple episodes throughout the 24-hour day is not recommended.'

citation.title: Adverse impact of polyphasic sleep patterns in humans: Report of the National Sleep Foundation sleep timing and variability consensus panel

notes: Evidence base small; excludes ordinary naps.

question: What sleep advice does NSF give for older adults?
keyResult: NSF Sleep Health and Aging Conference: essential recommendations for older adults focus on light exposure, physical activity, meal timing, environmental conditions, and sleep schedules; behavior change helped by tailored messaging and community support.

citation.authors: Koffel E, Ancoli-Israel S, Zee P, Dzierzewski JM
citation.title: Sleep health and aging: Recommendations for promoting healthy sleep among older adults: A National Sleep Foundation report

notes: Conference report; abstract gives no specific numbers. Older adults only.

newAdvice: Teens need later school start times; support them where you can (policy-level, context only).
question: What does NSF recommend to improve adolescent sleep at a societal level?
keyResult: NSF Adolescent Sleep Health Conference (22 experts): recommendations include implementing healthy school start times and adopting permanent standard time, raising awareness of sleep's impact on work and driving, and prioritizing sleep health equity; adolescents should be included as contributors.

citation.authors: Dautovich ND, Gunn HE, Dzierzewski JM, et al.
citation.title: Adolescent sleep health: Recommendations from the National Sleep Foundation

disagreement: Agrees with AAP 2014 (school start no earlier than 8:30 am).
notes: Policy-level, not individual advice; probably out of scope for the dataset except as context.

newAdvice: Put babies to sleep on their backs, on a firm flat surface, in your room but not in your bed.
question: How should infants be put to sleep safely?
keyResult: AAP 2022: safe sleep environment includes supine positioning; a firm, noninclined sleep surface; room sharing without bed sharing; avoidance of soft bedding and overheating. Additional SIDS risk reduction: human milk feeding; avoiding exposure to nicotine, alcohol, marijuana, opioids and illicit drugs; routine immunization; and pacifier use. About 3500 US infants die of sleep-related deaths each year.

citation.title: Sleep-Related Infant Deaths: Updated 2022 Recommendations for Reducing Infant Deaths in the Sleep Environment

notes: Infants only. Strong US policy; the dataset currently has no infant safe-sleep concept.
